crown.title: The Crown of the Mushroom King
crown.blurb: A shadowed wood, for the brave.

wp1.title: The Entrance
wp1.text:
A moth settles on the post beside you, its light guttering like a candle in a draft. “Traveler. Come close — closer, while my light still holds.” With every word the glow fades a little more. “I am the last of King Bolete’s messengers. The others, Lord Raggeth caught and snuffed out, one by one. I have flown a long way to find you, and I have not much left to burn.”

Behind it, the wood is wrong — grey, too silent, the smell of rot on the cold air.

“The king is dying. His crown is a ring of golden mushroom-caps — for what else would a mushroom-king wear? — and Lord Raggeth crept into the castle and tore three of those caps away. Where the crown goes dark, the forest follows. You can feel it already — the cold, the silence, the rot creeping root to root. By the last bell of nightfall the king’s heart will stop, and this wood will be Raggeth’s to rule: a kingdom of ash and bone. Three caps, scattered through the dark. Find them. Mend the crown. It is the only way left.”

It presses something small into your hand. “A honey-cake. There is little kindness left in this wood, traveler — spend yours well. It may cost more than you think. Go now. And trust no light but mine.”

wp2.title: Into the Forest
wp2.text:
You step off the road and the wood closes behind you like a held breath. The trees here are sick — bark gone black and weeping, leaves curled to ash. A small bird lies still in the path; the moth’s light passes over it and moves on, and does not look.

And the trees have faces — had you not noticed? Look again, as you walk. In the bark of the old ones: faces. Eyes and mouths and furrowed brows, watching you pass. “The forest’s old sentinels,” the moth says softly. “Awake since the first acorn fell. Once they sang to every traveler who came this way. But the king is dying, and one by one they have gone silent and still, their eyes drifting shut. They watch you now without a sound.”

The moth gathers what light it has, and tells you plainly what waits ahead, so you cannot say you were not warned:

“There are lights in this wood that wear a kind voice and a kind face, and they lead only to the bone-fields. There is a rot that spreads by touch and never, ever stops — it is the king’s dying, made into a thing that crawls. There are dead who do not rest, who guard to the grave what they died for. And there is Raggeth himself — who does not always kill what he catches. Sometimes he keeps it. Sometimes he turns it, and sends it back wearing your own face.”

Far off, a bell tolls — slow, and then slower. “The king’s heart,” the moth murmurs. “Hear how it fails. Three caps: one lies where a dying friend keeps watch, one where a false light feeds, one among the dead who were never avenged. This is the road ahead, traveler. It does not get kinder than here.”
wp2.prompt: Commit to the road ahead, or turn back?

choices.label: Go on into the dark
choices.text: You set your jaw and follow the leaning, half-rotted signpost deeper in. The moth’s light steadies, just a little, as if glad of company.

choices.label: Turn back — this is not my fight
choices.text: You turn for the road, and the daylight, and home. The moth does not plead. It only dims. Behind you, as you go, the last of its light gutters out, and the wood draws its silence closed over the king, and over the fox who waited, and over the dead who were never avenged. By morning there is no forest here at all — only ash, and bone, and a cold that came to stay. You were the last one it sent for.

wp3.title: The Great Old Tree
wp3.text:
Beneath the oldest tree, in the last patch the rot has not yet reached, a fox with one silver eye lies in the leaves. He is little more than bone and grey fur, and his breath comes shallow. He has guarded this place since before the tree stood tall — and now he is starving, for the blight has killed everything he might have hunted.

“I cannot move,” he says, and his voice is a thread. “I have not eaten in a week. I will not last the night.” Your hand finds the honey-cake. It is the only food you carry, and the night is long. This is the choice that sets your road.
wp3.prompt: Give him the honey-cake, or keep it?

choices.label: Give the honey-cake
choices.text: He eats slowly, gratefully, and when he is done his silver eye kindles like a struck coin. Strength returns to him by degrees. “Kindness,” he says softly, “is the first gold — rarer in this wood than any crown. You spent it on a dying old fox when you might have kept it for yourself.” From the moss he lifts a small golden cap and lays it in your palm. “I will not forget. When the dark is deepest, look for my eye.” He rises, unsteady but alive, and slips into the shadows ahead, going before you. You will not walk this wood alone.

choices.label: Keep it for yourself
choices.text:
You close your hand around the honey-cake and step around him. The fox says nothing — only watches you pass with his one silver eye, and you feel that eye on your back long after the trees have hidden him. There, in the leaves where he lies, the first golden cap gleams; it was the king’s, and the fox had no strength left to guard it. You lift it. Behind you, the old fox lowers his head to the cold ground; he will not see the morning.

And something in the wood feels the cruelty of it — a small coldness, given freely, in a place starved of warmth. It marks you. Not as his, not yet — the road ahead is still yours to choose — but the wood will remember the cold you carried in, and so, you suspect, will whatever stirred just now in the deep of the trees.

wp4.title: The Fork
wp4.text:
The path forks at a leaning, half-rotted post. To your right, the trail bends away gentle and even, winding off through the trees on level ground. Straight ahead, it pitches down into a dark hollow — stony, steep, and far longer, the harder of the two roads by a long mile. Both, the moth says, come at last to the same pond, and the sleeping king beyond it.

“Two roads, and both of them true,” the moth says, hovering close. “The right-hand way is kinder to your legs, and quicker to the king. The straight way drops into the low ground — steeper, longer, thick with his biting flies. But the king’s oldest friends keep to that road, and there are gifts on it found nowhere else. Few choose it now.” It steadies before your face. “The crown wants gold of three kinds, and one of them is cleverness — which is not cunning, child, but clear sight: knowing a true thing when you meet it, and choosing it with open eyes. So choose. Not the easy road, nor the hard one — your road. Only know which you take, and why.”
wp4.prompt: Which way do you take — the gentle right, or the rugged straight?

choices.label: Take the gentle path (right)
choices.advancePrompt: Take the right-hand trail and find the next post to continue.
choices.text: You choose the right-hand way, level and kind, and you choose it knowing — quicker to the king, with strength saved for whatever waits at the water. “Clear-eyed,” the moth says. “That is the second gold.” The Cap of Cleverness settles warm in your pocket — earned not by a clever tongue but by seeing plainly and choosing well. The gentle trail bends away to the right, and you follow it.

choices.label: Take the rugged path (straight ahead)
choices.advancePrompt: Take the steep path straight ahead and find the first post on the rugged road.
choices.text: You choose the hard road — straight on, down into the stony hollow, the longer and steeper way — and you choose it knowing exactly what it costs, for the gifts the king’s old friends keep there. “Clear-eyed, and bold with it,” the moth says, half a laugh and half a worry. “That is the second gold — and you’ll have need of the rest before this road is done.” The Cap of Cleverness settles warm in your pocket. The trail pitches down before you into the dark.

scenes.text:
The trees give way to a small graveyard — a dozen old stones, leaning every which way in the grey light. These are the king’s knights, the last of the old mushroom-guard, who stood against Raggeth an age ago and fell to the last, and were never avenged. The wood forgot them. The rot has not — it creeps among the stones like spilled ink.

At the center stands one great cracked stone, and at its foot a candle, long gone cold. “The last cap is here,” the moth breathes, “in the keeping of the dead. They will not give it to the timid. You must wake their captain — and you must not look away when he wakes.”
scenes.prompt: Light the candle and wake the guardian, or tiptoe past?

choices.label: Light the candle
choices.text: Your hands shake so badly you can barely breathe on the wick — but it catches, one small gold flame in a sea of grey. The great stone splits. Something rises from it: a knight of blackened oak and toadstool, vast, its eyes two coals, an age of grief in its ruined face. It would be so easy to run. You do not run. For a long, cold moment the dead captain weighs you — then slowly bows. “Courage,” it says, in a voice like a closing tomb, “is the last gold, and it is bought with fear, not the lack of it.” It lays the third cap in your hand, and then it does not sink back. It takes up its broken sword and falls in at your shoulder. “We could not save the king. We will see you to him. And when you face Raggeth — for you will — we will not look away, and neither will you.” You walk on with a dead knight at your side.

choices.label: Tiptoe quietly past
choices.text: You cannot do it. You hold your breath and slip between the graves, quiet as the dead themselves, and you do not light the candle, and you do not wake the captain. The last cap you find at the graveyard’s edge, set upon a small stone — a young knight’s grave, one who fell too soon. You lift it with hands that will not stop shaking, and all across that little ground you feel the weight of eyes that hoped for more from you, and let you pass anyway. No knight rises to walk with you. But the fox is still ahead, and the moth is still at your shoulder, and that will have to be enough.

scenes.text:
The trees give way to a small graveyard — the king’s old knights, who stood against Raggeth an age ago and fell, and were never avenged. The rot creeps among the stones. And the dead feel you the moment you step in — not the gold you carry, but the cold you carry: the small cruelty of the fox left to die on the road behind you, the first dark thing the wood has felt in you.

The great cracked stone splits, and the captain rises, two coals for eyes, and looks at that coldness with something worse than anger — recognition. “We died to keep the dark out of this wood,” it says, “and here it walks in, wearing a child’s face, carrying the king’s own gold.” It lifts the cold dead candle from the stone and holds it out. “This is the cure, and it is cruel. Light it, and face what you did on the road — it will burn like a little dying, but you will come back yourself. Or turn from us and keep the cold, and carry it on to the pond — and we will not stop you, for you will already be his.”
scenes.prompt: Light the candle and face what you did, or turn from the dead?

choices.label: Light the candle — face what you did
choices.text: You touch the flame to the wick, and it catches — and the cold in you catches with it, and burns. It is a little death: you go down on the cold ground, and you come back up scarred, and shaking, and yourself again. The Cap of Courage is in your hand. “Courage,” the captain says, quieter now, “is bought with fear — and sometimes with worse. You let something die on the road, and you came back to mourn it. Few do. Go on — a Hero still, though a marked one.”

choices.label: Turn from the dead and keep the cold
choices.text: You close your hand over the cold in your chest and back away from the candle and its cruel little fire. “Then carry it,” the captain says, and there is no anger left, only a vast tiredness. The third cap it sets on the nearest stone; you take it, because some part of you still counts to three. The dead sink down and do not watch you go. The cold has the whole of you now, and the road ahead looks like something owed to you. You climb toward the pond — and toward the one whose road you have chosen without ever being asked.

wp6.title: The Way to the Pond
wp6.text:
Three caps, cold in your hand, and the wood gone nearly black around you. The moth’s light is a dying ember now; it can barely lift from your shoulder. The bell — the king’s heart — tolls once more, so faint you feel it more than hear it, and the silence that follows runs on too long before the next.

“Hurry,” the moth breathes. “He is almost gone. The path climbs from here — the pond lies above us, at the top of the wood, where the forest was born, and where, tonight, it may die.” The signpost points the way up into the dark. You climb.

scenes.text: The rugged way tips downward past a leaning marker, into a hollow of black trees you cannot see the bottom of. The fox pads up beside you, ears pricked, glad of the hard road. “The old way,” he says, dry and warm. “The way of the king’s friends. Few take it now.” Below, the trail drops away into shadow.
scenes.prompt: Send the fox ahead to scout, or keep him close?

choices.label: Send him ahead to scout
choices.text: He slips into the dark to read the way for you. You walk the drop alone a while — but you will know what is coming.

choices.label: Keep him close
choices.text: You would rather face it together than know it early. He stays at your heel, and you go down into the hollow side by side.

scenes.advancePrompt: Head down into the hollow and find the next post on the rugged road.

scenes.text: The rugged way tips downward past a leaning marker, into a hollow of black trees you cannot see the bottom of. You reach the marker alone — no one to send ahead, no one to walk beside. The hollow waits below, and the cold comes up out of it to meet you.
scenes.prompt: Press on now, or steady yourself first?

choices.label: Press on while you’ve nerve
choices.text: You don’t give the dark time to grow in your mind. Down you go.

choices.label: Take a breath at the marker
choices.text: You gather yourself a moment before the drop. Slower — but your heart is your own.

The descent ends, and the trail bends away to your right, leveling out toward a stand of distant pines — the long flat to the spring begins here, and the climb to the king is somewhere far ahead. The fox trots the bend with you, ranging ahead and circling back, glad of the easy ground. At your feet, among the leaf-litter, lie fallen branches — stout, straight, stick-high.
scenes.prompt: Take up a walking stick for the road, or travel light?

choices.label: Take a stick
choices.text: You choose a good straight one, test your weight on it, tuck it under your arm. It’s nothing now, here on the flat — but there’s a hill between you and the king.

choices.label: Travel light
choices.text: Your hands are free and your step is quick, and the flat is easy going. You don’t think about the climb yet.

The flat brings you in among the only pines on the walk — green, unrotted, resinous — where a spring bubbles up clear among the roots and one old pine creaks like a slow voice. The fox laps once at the pool and settles at its edge, ears soft, as if he knows this place. Kneel at the pool and the creaking pine bends low, and the fairy speaks — tiny, ancient, kind. “A traveler, on the king’s road, and brave for the stony way. Drink. Fill your flask. The spring feeds the king’s own heart-well, and it is the last clean water in the wood.”

You drink — so cold it aches, so clean it steadies you — and fill the fairy’s flask. Then she says: “I’ll give you one thing more to carry. Choose.”
scenes.prompt: The fairy’s parting gift — which do you ask for?

choices.label: Ask for a number to remember
choices.text: “Then hold this,” she whispers. “Seven. When you stand before the dark one and must name the watching faces of the wood, you will be glad you carried it. Seven. Don’t let the fear knock it loose.” You don’t know yet what it means — but you will hold it.

choices.label: Ask for a blessing of strength
choices.text: “Then take strength instead,” she says, and the cold water warms in you, steadying your legs for the long climb and the longer dark. You’ll feel it carrying you up the hill — but you’ll have to count the faces yourself, and trust your own tally.

The path runs into a grove thick with carved faces — the watching wood, more awake here near the spring’s clean magic, eyes opening as you pass. The fox pads close to your leg, unbothered; they know him too. “A friend of the king,” they murmur, trunk to trunk. “The fairy spoke of you. We have two gifts, and you may take one.”

choices.label: Ask the grove for strength on the road
choices.text: Their warmth pours into you for what’s to come — the climb, and the dark beyond it. You’ll feel it carrying you up the hill.

choices.label: Ask the grove to keep watch at your back
choices.text: “Then we will hold the dark behind you, as far as we can reach.” Their watching cousins line the road ahead; on the long walk to Raggeth, the dark will press less close at your heels.

wp7.title: The Pond
wp7.text: The climb brings you out at the pond — the old heart-well of the forest, whose waters rise and fall with the king’s own life.

seasonalIntro.text: The water lies black and brimming and still — yet no stars float in it, for the sky itself has gone dark. “The last of the king’s strength,” the moth murmurs, “pooled here, and waiting, while it holds.”

Where deep water should be there is only a cracked and shrinking hollow, a last puddle sinking into mud. “The pond drains as the king does,” the moth breathes. “Nearly empty now. We are nearly too late.”

scenes.textCont: You kneel at the king’s toadstool throne and show him the three golden caps — kindness, cleverness, courage, gathered the length of the wood. The dim old eyes find them, and something like dawn moves across his ruined face. “All three. Then you have already done a brave and a great thing — and what comes next is yours to choose.” His cracked hand lifts. “Set these in my crown now, and I am saved: the rot will heal, and you may go home in honor, your task done. No one could ask more of you.” His voice drops. “But know this before you choose. Raggeth still lives, deep in the wood, and he holds the heart of my crown — the last and truest gold. Save me now, and you save me for your lifetime. End him, and you save this wood forever. There is no shame in either road.”
scenes.prompt: Rest your quest here with honor, or go on to end Raggeth forever?

choices.label: Set the caps in the crown — your task is done
Keep the caps, and go end Raggeth forever
choices.text:
“Then keep the gold,” the king says. “You’ll need it for what waits.” The moth flutters down before your face, its small light trembling. “This is where I must leave you. I cannot go where he is — his dark would snuff me out in a breath. You go alone from here.”

“But listen first, for this is how he is beaten. Raggeth’s rot is bound to this wood by the wood’s own count — and the wood will tell you the numbers, if you walk its whole length and pay attention. As you go, count three things. The resting-benches along the road — not these here by the pond, mind, but the ones from here onward to his hut. The feast-tables in the bright meadow. And the watching faces where the trail cuts through the fallen tree. Three true numbers. Carry them to him, name them aloud, and his binding breaks. You cannot learn them by cutting across — only by walking the road. So walk it.”

It rests a moment against your cheek, light as ash. “Follow the red tree-arrows, and only them. You’ll see his hut across the hollow before the path reaches it; never leave the markers — the wood between is where the bones are. Go bravely. And come back.” The light lifts away, and then the moth is gone, and for the first time all night, you are alone.

endingVariants.text: One by one you press the golden caps home into the bare ring of the crown, and light runs through it and steadies the king — but you flinched, once, on the way here, when it counted, and the ending is a quieter one. The king lives; the wood will live. No retinue of friends comes to walk you out; the moth lights you to the road, faithful to the last, and that is enough, and it is a little lonely. “You saved my forest,” the king says, gentler than a bell. “Go home in honor — and be a little braver next time. There is always a next time, in a wood.” The face-trees open their eyes as you pass, and watch you go, and do not quite smile. Your story is complete.

One by one you press the golden caps home into the bare ring of the king’s crown — and the moment the third is set, light runs through it like dawn through water, and does not stop. It pours from the crown into the king, into the throne, into the roots, out through the whole black wood. King Bolete straightens, grey going green, his crown blazing gold; the rot draws back into the earth; and all around the pond, the dying simply stops. The heart-well answers him, its waters clearing and rising. The king stands — tall, and shining, and saved — and his voice is no longer a whisper but a bell: “You carried my crown out of the dark and made me whole. Go home in honor, brave one. The wood will sing your name.” As you walk back down through the trees, the forest is already waking around you — green returning, birdsong, the face-trees opening their eyes to watch you pass and, one by one, beginning to smile. You saved the king. You saved the forest. Your story is complete.

Far off in the deep wood a thin green smoke still rises — Raggeth, unbeaten, biding. But that is a tale for another brave soul, another day. Tonight, you have won.

scenes.textCont:
On a toadstool throne at the water’s edge sits King Bolete — grey to the bone, cracked like old wood — and his failing eyes find the cold you carried past the dead and never burned away. “Ah,” he breathes, and closes them. “So that is how it is.”

[PAWN’S ROAD — the sealed-pawn finale (serve / enslaved) is not yet written. This placeholder ends the walk cleanly so the road never dead-ends.]

ending.note: 🩸 The Pawn’s Road — finale to be written

exits.label: The wood grants one last mercy — flee
exits.reveal: You turn from the throne and carry the cold caps back out of the wood, and the dark closes behind you. The true ending of the Pawn’s Road — to serve, and be kept — is still to be written. For now, you walk out, and the wood waits.

rg_road.title: Into the Deep Wood
rg_road.text: You cross from the pond and the red markers take you down into the deep wood — darker here than anywhere, no moth, no king, no fox, only you and the red arrows nailed to the black trees, one and then the next. The dark does not last. The trees thin, the ground rises in a long gentle climb, and the path carries you up, out of the gloom, toward a growing light ahead.

variants.text: And the dark keeps its distance as you go — the grove’s watching cousins lining the way, holding it back from your heels.

rg_meadow.title: The Wildflower Meadow
rg_meadow.text:
You come out into sudden light: a wide wildflower meadow, warm and gold and humming with bees, lovely past belief so near the dark one’s house. And Raggeth’s voice drifts sweet across it: “There now. Rest. You’ve come so far. The king has waited this long; he can wait a while more.” Benches sit among the flowers, set just so, inviting.

[Count the resting-benches as you go — and remember, only those from the pond onward, never the pond’s own.]

rg_picnic.title: The Picnic Place
rg_picnic.text:
The path leads on to a quiet picnic place, tables in the warm gold light, and the pull to stop is strong — the wood’s craftiest trick, not to scare you back but to keep you.

[Count the feast-tables here in the meadow.]
rg_picnic.prompt: Rest a moment, then rise — or march straight through?

choices.label: Rest a moment, then walk on
choices.text: You sit, you breathe, you let your legs recover — and then you stand and go, because no meadow will make you forget the grey king and the dying wood. Resting was wise; rising was braver.

choices.label: March straight through
choices.text: You don’t trust the warmth for a heartbeat; you keep your eyes on the red arrows and go — counting the tables as you pass, careful not to lose the number in your hurry.

rg_faces.title: The Fallen-Tree Faces
rg_faces.text:
The light dies behind you, the trees close in, and the trail comes to a great fallen tree it cuts straight through — and here the carved faces crowd thickest, watching from every trunk around the gap.

[Count the watching faces here at the fallen tree.]

variants.text: And you understand, now, what the fairy meant — count them, and you will find she gave you the truth.

rg_lair.title: The Lair in Sight
rg_lair.text: Through a gap you see it across the hollow — the black hut, the smoking cauldron. Close. The path bends the long way round, and the cold voice wheedles: “Why walk so far? The hut is just there. Cut across; save your legs. Come straight to me.” But you remember the bones — and you remember you cannot know the wood’s numbers without walking its whole road.
rg_lair.prompt: Stay on the markers, or cut across?

choices.label: Stay on the red markers
choices.text: You keep the path, down and around, and Raggeth’s voice sours from coaxing to a hiss as he sees you won’t be tricked.

choices.label: Cut across toward the hut
choices.text: You step off the markers toward the close, easy hut — and the ground is not ground. The dark between the trees is the bone-field; it drags at your feet, and the corpse-light kindles ahead, smiling. This is how he takes travelers. The wood has you — but not yet. And you’d have reached him without the numbers, and lost anyway.

rg_hut.title: The Hut and the Hatch
rg_hut.buildNote: REAL-WORLD: put a physical 'KEEP CLOSED' sign on the actual hut hatch — there may be real wasps in there.
rg_hut.text: The long way round brings you to the hut at last — small and mean and very old, its boards weeping rot, the cauldron seething before it. Raggeth is a cold thinness in the air. On the hut’s face is a small black hatch, and the voice turns silky: “There’s a treasure behind that hatch — the king’s last gold, perhaps. Open it. Go on — open it, and see.”
rg_hut.prompt: Open the hatch, or leave it?

choices.label: Leave the hatch shut
choices.text: You don’t touch it. The answer was never behind a door he wants you to open. Raggeth’s voice curdles with annoyance.

choices.label: Open the hatch
choices.advanceLabel: Leave the hatch shut — back away
choices.text: Your hand goes to the latch — and a night’s worth of warnings catch you a beat too late: the hatch is not where the treasure is. It’s where his swarm is. Get back!

rg_confront.title: The Count Is the Weapon
rg_confront.text:
“So. The king’s little counter, come to my door.” The cauldron seethes, the rot crawling up green and sick. And you understand what the moth meant: the rot is bound to the wood by the wood’s own count, and to break it you must name the three true numbers aloud — the benches, the tables, the faces.

First: the resting-benches along the road, counting only from the pond onward.
rg_confront.prompt: Name the number of resting-benches (from the pond onward).

choices.label: Four
hints: The cauldron flares; Raggeth laughs. “You didn’t walk my road — you guessed.” Picture the road from the pond: the benches among the wildflowers, the benches by the picnic place. Count them again — only those from the pond onward, not the pond’s own.
It flares higher, and the wood darkens a notch. Walk it again in your mind, bench by bench, from the moment you left the pond to his door. Name that number.
Higher still — but steady. The resting-benches, from the pond onward. Say the true number, and the blow lands.

choices.label: Five
choices.text: “Five,” you say — and the first true number lands like a hammer-blow. The cauldron cracks; the green boil shudders; Raggeth’s sneer falters.

rg_ward2.title: The Second Number
rg_ward2.text: “Lucky,” Raggeth hisses, but the cold has thinned. The second number now: the feast-tables in the bright meadow.
rg_ward2.prompt: Name the number of feast-tables in the meadow.

choices.label: Three
hints: The rot surges back up the gold. “Guessing again,” Raggeth purrs. The picnic place — the feast-tables in the warm gold light, where the meadow begged you to stay. Count them again.
It flares, and the dark leans closer. Only the meadow’s tables, mind. Name them true.
Almost. The feast-tables of the bright meadow. The number is waiting; say it.

choices.label: Four
choices.text: “Four,” you say — and the second number lands; the cauldron splits further, and Raggeth’s voice climbs toward a snarl.

It flares, and the dark leans closer. Only the meadow’s tables, mind. Name them true.

rg_ward3.title: The Last Number
rg_ward3.text: The cauldron is cracked rim to foot now, leaking green; Raggeth is a fury with no warmth left. One number remains — the watching faces at the cut through the fallen tree.

variants.text: The fairy’s word returns to you, clear as her cold spring: seven. You carried it for exactly this moment. Don’t let his snarling knock it loose.
Count them once more in your memory — the faces crowded thick where the great trunk had fallen across the path.

rg_ward3.prompt: Name the number of watching faces at the fallen tree.

choices.label: Five
hints: The cauldron screams and gutters. The faces — where the trail cut through the great fallen tree, crowded thick in every trunk around the gap. Count them again.
It flares; the wood groans. Only the fallen-tree faces. If the fairy gave you her number, trust it now.
Almost. The watching faces at the fallen tree. Name the last true number, and his binding breaks.

endingVariants.text: “Five, and four, and seven,” you say — and the wood’s own count closes around Raggeth like a fist. The cauldron screams and splits from rim to foot; the rot pours out into the starving ground and is gone; and Raggeth — the cold, the thinness, the dry voice — comes apart with his pot, unraveling into nothing with one last astonished sigh. Far off you hear the watching faces, every one, waking and glad. From the wreck you lift the last and truest gold — the heart of the king’s crown, that Raggeth held. You carry it home through a wood already greening behind you, and at the castle you set the three caps and the heart together into the crown, and it is whole — forever whole, this time — and King Bolete rises shining, and the long night ends in dawn. The forest is reborn, and it will not forget the one who saved it.

“Five, and four, and seven,” you say at last — and the wood’s own count closes around Raggeth, though you reached it the hard way, by guess and recount, the wood darkening at each wrong word. The cauldron screams and splits; the rot drains into the ground; and Raggeth comes apart with his pot, unraveling into nothing. The wood will live, and the king will rise. But it was clumsy and costly, and you’ll always know there was a cleaner road — that a sharper eye on the long walk would have spared the dark its last gloating. Still: you walked the whole dark way, you did not give in, and you named it true. That is no small thing. From the wreck you lift the heart of the crown; the three caps and the heart make it whole, and the king rises, and dawn comes.
